title: Spinosaurus Lived Underwater? #1 Was Solved With WWII Radar Math
description: A new Yale-led study says Spinosaurus, the biggest meat-eating dinosaur ever found, spent most of its life submerged. We count down five secrets of this 50-foot river monster, from fossils destroyed by bombs in 1944 to a fish-like tail, penguin-like bones, and the World War Two radar math that may finally settle the fight.
sources: ScienceDaily / Yale University (25 Oct 2026) New evidence suggests Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater (Gordon, Freisem, Griffin, Gauthier, Bhullar, Current Biology, 'Limb proportions predict aquatic habits and soft-tissue flippers in extinct amniotes', doi 10.1016/j.cub.2025.10.068; 11,000+ measurements; >90% accuracy; WWII radar-blip statistical method; Spinosaurus ~113–94 million years ago; 'vast majority of its time submerged'; does not settle how it hunted) — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261024221956.htm

Linda Hall Library: Ernst Stromer (Jan 1911 Bahariya limb bones, first dinosaur bones in Egypt; 1912 partial skeleton by Richard Markgraf; spines up to a meter; named 1915; RAF raid on Munich 25 April 1944 destroyed collection; director refused to move it) — https://www.lindahall.org/ernst-stromer/

National Geographic (2020) Bizarre Spinosaurus makes history as first known swimming dinosaur (Ibrahim et al., Nature; ~50 ft, ~7 tons, longer than adult T. rex; 6-ft sail; 2008 Erfoud meeting; 2014 Science skeleton; Kem Kem 95–100 million years, river system; 30+ tail vertebrae by end of 2018; struts nearly 2 ft; Pierce & Lauder robot: >8x thrust, twice as efficient; quotes) — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/first-spinosaurus-tail-found-confirms-dinosaur-was-swimming

University of Cambridge (2022) Dense bones allowed Spinosaurus to hunt underwater (Fabbri, Navalón, Benson et al., Nature, doi 10.1038/s41586-022-04528-0; 250 species; penguins, hippos, alligators; Baryonyx dense, Suchomimus lighter; bottom-walking like hippos; lungfishes, coelacanths) — https://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/dense-bones-allowed-spinosaurus-to-hunt-underwater

University of Chicago (2022) Spinosaurus is not an aquatic dinosaur (Sereno et al., eLife, 30 Nov 2022; too buoyant; 15–25x tail power needed to submerge; swimming power ~10x less than alligator; sail made it unstable; wading) — https://biologicalsciences.uchicago.edu/news/spinosaurus-not-aquatic

scenes.say: Scientists just ran the numbers. The biggest meat-eating dinosaur ever found lived mostly underwater.

scenes.label: New study
scenes.say: Okay, so that's not a movie pitch. A Yale-led team published it, and it's making headlines this week.

scenes.label: Longer than T. rex
scenes.say: And this animal was longer than an adult T. rex. Picture that thing slipping under a river without a ripple.

scenes.label: The big fight
scenes.say: But not every scientist agrees. And at the very end, I'll show you who's winning the fight.

scenes.label: 5 secrets
scenes.say: So today, five secrets of Spinosaurus. Each one stranger than the last.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: And stay for number one. The answer came from math invented in World War Two, to spot enemy planes on radar.

scenes.label: Lost in a war
scenes.say: Number five. The first Spinosaurus ever found was blown up.

scenes.label: Egypt, 1911
scenes.say: Rewind to January 1911. A German scientist named Ernst Stromer is digging in Egypt's Western Desert, at a place called Bahariya.

scenes.label: First in Egypt
scenes.say: He finds three huge limb bones. They're the first dinosaur bones ever dug up in Egypt.

scenes.label: Spines up to 1 m
scenes.say: A year later, his fossil collector finds more. A lower jaw, teeth, and backbones with spines up to a meter long.

scenes.label: Spine lizard
scenes.say: Spines sticking straight up, like they held up a sail. In 1915, Stromer names it Spinosaurus. Spine lizard.
Its full name was Spinosaurus aegyptiacus. The Egyptian spine lizard. Weird bones, weird name, and nobody knew what it did.
He ships the bones home to a museum in Munich. And for almost thirty years, that's where they stay.

scenes.label: He said no
scenes.say: Then World War Two comes. Stromer begs the museum director to move the fossils somewhere safe. The director says no.

scenes.label: 25 April 1944
scenes.say: On April 25, 1944, hundreds of British bombers hit Munich. The museum takes a direct hit.

scenes.label: All gone
scenes.say: Every bone is gone. The only real proof Spinosaurus existed? Old drawings and photos.
And here's a detail that makes it worse. The danger was known. Stromer had warned them, and still, nothing was saved.
Think about that. For decades, the world's strangest dinosaur was basically a rumor on paper.

scenes.label: A true giant
scenes.say: Number four. It was a giant. Like, bigger than you're imagining.

scenes.label: Morocco, 2008
scenes.say: Fast forward to 2008. A young paleontologist, Nizar Ibrahim, is in a desert town in Morocco.

scenes.label: Lucky meeting
scenes.say: A local man shows him some bones he dug up. They might be Spinosaurus. And it turns out, they are.

scenes.label: 2014 skeleton
scenes.say: In 2014, Ibrahim's team describes a new skeleton. Finally, a replacement for the bones lost in the war.

scenes.label: ~50 feet, ~7 tons
scenes.say: Now the size. About 50 feet long and around seven tons. That's longer than an adult T. rex. Yep. The most famous dinosaur on Earth would lose the length contest.

scenes.label: 6-foot sail
scenes.say: And on its back, a sail about six feet tall. Taller than most grown-ups. Just sitting up there.

scenes.label: Croc snout
scenes.say: Plus a long snout like a crocodile, packed with cone-shaped teeth. Perfect for grabbing slippery fish.

scenes.label: Sawfish lunch
scenes.say: Scientists even picture it hunting Onchopristis, a prehistoric sawfish. A fish with a giant saw on its face. Yeah, that was lunch.
So what's a seven-ton monster with a fish-grabbing face doing in the desert? Here's the twist. It wasn't a desert back then.

scenes.label: A fish tail
scenes.say: Number three. This dinosaur had a tail like a fish.

scenes.label: A giant river
scenes.say: About 95 to 100 million years ago, this part of Morocco was a huge river system. Water everywhere.

scenes.label: 30+ tail bones
scenes.say: Ibrahim's team kept digging. By the end of 2018, they'd pulled up more than 30 tail bones.

scenes.label: An oar
scenes.say: And the tail was weird. Bony struts almost two feet long stuck out of it, making it tall and flat. Like an oar.

scenes.label: Built to wiggle
scenes.say: Near the tip, the bones barely locked together. So the tail could bend and wave, side to side, pushing through water.

scenes.label: Five tables
scenes.say: The tail was so long, the team needed five tables just to lay it out. Five tables. For one tail.
Ibrahim said it best. This was basically a dinosaur trying to build a fish tail.

scenes.label: Most extreme
scenes.say: The study in the journal Nature called it the most extreme water adaptation ever seen in a large dinosaur.
Another expert put it simply. Spinosaurus is even weirder than we thought it was.

scenes.label: Robot test
scenes.say: So Harvard scientists built a model of it. Then they hooked it to a swimming robot in a water tank.
They tested it against the tails of two other meat-eating dinosaurs. Normal land tails.

scenes.label: 8x the thrust
scenes.say: The result? The Spinosaurus tail pushed more than eight times harder through water. And twice as efficiently.
One scientist reacted with, quote, it's unbelievable. Okay. But a good tail doesn't prove you live underwater. Right?

scenes.label: Penguin bones
scenes.say: Number two. Its bones were built like a penguin's.

scenes.label: Solid vs hollow
scenes.say: Here's a cool trick. Animals that dive for food usually have solid, heavy bones. Land animals have hollow ones.

scenes.label: Built-in weights
scenes.say: Heavy bones work like a diver's weight belt. Hippos have them. Penguins have them. They help you sink.

scenes.label: 250 species
scenes.say: In 2022, a team from the Field Museum, Cambridge and Oxford sliced into the bones of 250 species, alive and extinct.

scenes.label: Dense bones
scenes.say: Spinosaurus? Super dense bones. Like a penguin. Like a hippo. Like an alligator.

scenes.label: Bone has memory
scenes.say: One scientist said it perfectly. Bone has memory. It remembers how an animal lived, millions of years later.

scenes.label: Cousin #1
scenes.say: Its cousin Baryonyx had dense bones too. So it probably went under the water as well.

scenes.label: Cousin #2
scenes.say: But another cousin, Suchomimus, had lighter, hollow bones. Same fishy snout, but it probably waded instead.

scenes.label: River walker
scenes.say: So the researchers pictured Spinosaurus walking along the river bottom, kind of like a hippo, swishing that tail.

scenes.label: On the menu
scenes.say: Hunting big fish, like ancient lungfish and coelacanths. Ambush from below. Sounds settled, right? Swimming dinosaur, case closed. Nope. This is where it gets messy.

scenes.label: Not aquatic?
scenes.say: Because in November 2022, another team fired back. Their paper's title? Spinosaurus is not an aquatic dinosaur.

scenes.label: Too floaty
scenes.say: Paul Sereno's team at the University of Chicago did the math. They said Spinosaurus floated too well to stay under.

scenes.label: 15-25x short
scenes.say: To sink itself, it would need 15 to 25 times more power than its tail could make. And it swam far weaker than an alligator.

scenes.label: Tippy sail
scenes.say: Worse, that giant sail made it tippy. It would struggle to stay upright in deep water.

scenes.label: Giant heron
scenes.say: Their picture? A giant wading bird. Standing in the shallows, snatching fish. Like a seven-ton heron.

scenes.label: Heavy, not diving
scenes.say: Sereno even said the solid leg bones weren't ballast for swimming. They were there to hold up the beast's huge weight.
So which is it? Underwater hunter or giant wading bird? Comment your guess before number one.

scenes.label: War math
scenes.say: Number one. And this is the one I promised. The answer came from war math.

scenes.label: Plane or noise?
scenes.say: During World War Two, radar operators had a problem. Is that blip on the screen an enemy plane? Or just noise? So they built a math method to tell real signals from fake ones.

scenes.label: Yale study
scenes.say: A Yale-led team, led by Caleb Gordon, borrowed that same old method for a brand new study.

scenes.label: 11,000+ measurements
scenes.say: They took more than 11,000 measurements, from living animals and extinct ones.
Then they trained a computer on living animals, whose lifestyles we already know. Swimmers, waders and walkers.

scenes.label: 90%+ accurate
scenes.say: The test worked. It guessed whether an animal had flippers, or was highly aquatic, with more than 90 percent accuracy.

scenes.label: Arms tell all
scenes.say: Fun detail. The arms turned out to be the best clue. Front limb proportions were especially good at telling swimmers from walkers.

scenes.label: Mostly submerged
scenes.say: Then they fed it Spinosaurus. The verdict? Highly aquatic. Spending the vast majority of its time submerged.

scenes.label: Back to land
scenes.say: And the same model checked older sea reptiles too. Some, called mesosaurs, still came back to land. Kind of like an alligator or a platypus.

scenes.label: Not over yet
scenes.say: But here's the honest part. Even this study doesn't settle exactly how Spinosaurus hunted. The fight isn't over.

scenes.label: 113-94 million yrs
scenes.say: Think about it. This animal lived 113 to 94 million years ago. And we're still arguing about how it lived.
Its first bones were bombed. Its second skeleton was found by luck. And now war math is reading its bones.

scenes.label: Your vote?
scenes.say: So what do you think? Underwater hunter, or seven-ton heron? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: WWII Radar Math Says Spinosaurus Lived Underwater
short.description: A new Yale-led study used a World War Two radar statistics method on 11,000+ bone measurements and concluded Spinosaurus spent most of its time submerged. Others say it only waded. Sources: Gordon et al., Current Biology; Sereno et al. 2022, eLife; National Geographic.

scenes.say: Scientists used World War Two radar math to read a dinosaur's bones.
Radar operators back then needed to tell a real enemy plane from random noise. So they built a math trick for it.
Decades later, a Yale-led team used it on more than 11,000 bone measurements from living and extinct animals.
Trained on living swimmers and walkers, their model guessed water lifestyles with more than 90 percent accuracy.
Then they tested Spinosaurus. Fifty feet long, seven tons, longer than T. rex. Verdict? It spent most of its life underwater.
But other scientists say it floated too well to dive, and just waded like a giant heron. Which side are you on? Because yes,
scientists used World War Two radar math to read a dinosaur's bones.
